newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Easier Brazil reforms done, hard ones still to go.
newsitem.headline: Easier Brazil reforms done, hard ones still to go.

text.p: The Brazilian government finished the first, "easier" half of its reform program late Wednesday when the Senate approved a bill regulating the opening up of the oil and gas industries to competition.

The legislation was the last of several that set down the rules for private companies operating in Brazil's underdeveloped telecommunications, power and petroleum sectors and pave the way for multi-billion-dollar privatizations.

But more controversial structural reforms, which are seen as essential to Brazil's long-term economic prospects, have been stuck in Congress for more than two years and are unlikely to be fully implemented before next year's elections, analysts said.

Unlike the moves to dismantle its monopolies, the government's civil service and pension reforms threaten to do away with the kind of political patronage and privileges that sustain Brazil's status quo.

"It's going to be very hard for the government to get the civil service and pension reforms through," said Alexandre Barros of consultants Early Warning. "Both strike at the heart of the Brazilian elite, especially those who control Congress."
In the absence of structural reform, the government has been forced into a political battle to renew its Fiscal Stabilization Fund which enables it to cover shortfalls in the federal budget.
A bill extending the fund until 1999 was approved in a first vote in the Chamber of Deputies Wednesday, despite opposition from the country's mayors who lose out under its terms.
Officials say they would not have to take emergency steps like that if the reforms were in place.

The civil service reform bill -- which seeks to streamline Brazil's bloated public sector and save the government the equivalent of 0.8 percent of gross domestic product -- has yet to face its stiffest test in the Chamber of Deputies.

The lower house is expected to approve the bill itself in August when it comes up for a second full vote. But the government will struggle to defeat an opposition amendment that would prevent mass dismissals of workers.
Government officials say they may scrap the reform altogether if the amendment is not defeated, resorting instead to emergency measures to cut jobs and spending.
An equally important -- but just as slow -- reform of the social security system cleared a hurdle in Congress Thursday when it was approved in a Senate committee.

That vote was only made possible, however, when the government settled for a latest compromise over the bill, agreeing that retired civil servants would be entitled to all or some of pay increases awarded to workers.

If approved in the upper house, the pension bill faces the daunting prospect of another round of voting in the Chamber of Deputies where it was stripped of its main points last year by lawmakers with powerful backers in the civil service.

"The bill...is a reform, although not how the government planned it," political columnist Tereza Cruvinel wrote in newspaper O Globo. "It remains to be seen if the Chamber of Deputies will keep it as it is."

Most observers say President Fernando Henrique Cardoso will find it increasingly difficult to keep a grip on his multi-party alliance in the Chamber of Deputies as next year's presidential, congressional and state governorship elections loom ever larger.
Reforms which have made only painstaking progress through Congress over the last two years are unlikely to fair any better in the volatile run-up to polling day on October 3, 1998.
But political analyst Barros said much of the blame for the government's reform difficulties lay with the president and his overblown efforts not to make enemies in Congress.

"When you want reform, you have be like Margaret Thatcher: either you're with us or against us," Barros said, refering to Britain's former prime minister, renowned for her determination. "But the Fernando Henrique government wants to please everyone."
